How Big Should My Koi Pond Be?

Koi Feeding Guide – Feeding Koi Fish, What to Feed & Tips – Champion Nishikigoi

facts.fact: Koi grow large: adults over 20 inches need depth and horizontal swimming room.
A koi pond expert says he personally avoids building koi ponds under 2,000 gallons.
A 204-litre pond (about 90 x 75 x 30 cm deep) is definitely too small for koi, according to Practical Fishkeeping's Jeremy Gay.
Cotswold Koi says a pond of about 600 to 1,000 gallons may be enough for 5 to 10 koi.
For larger groups, Cotswold Koi suggests roughly 100 to 500 gallons of water per koi.
Cotswold Koi recommends a pond depth of at least 3 to 4 feet, mainly for stable temperature and predator protection.
A Vietnamese guide recommends a glass tank of at least 1.2 m so koi have room to swim.
The same guide recommends tempered glass at least 10 mm thick, since thinner glass can break from water pressure or impact.
Suggested water parameters for koi in the Vietnamese guide are 22–28 °C, pH 7–7.5 and dissolved oxygen about 7–9 mg/L.
Merck says dissolved oxygen above 5 mg/L is optimal for most finfish, and fish are stressed below 5 mg/L.
Rule of thumb for stocking: about 1 inch of fish per 10 gallons, treated only as a starting point.
Another rule of thumb: no more than four koi per 1,000 gallons, to limit pheromone and toxin buildup.
Circulate the whole pond volume about once an hour.
An oversized filter supports a higher fish load, and extra aeration such as air pumps lets a pond safely hold more fish.
Choose filters that are easy to clean often, such as by backflushing. Owners should be able to clean the filter at least monthly.
Weekly backflushing and partial water changes are recommended. Skimmers and bottom drains remove waste before it settles as sludge.
A properly sized UV clarifier helps control algae.
Plant one bog or oxygenating plant per 10 square feet of surface, and let waterlilies cover up to 50% of the surface.
Choose a filter whose capacity matches the tank volume. The guide gives no specific flow rate.
Feed about 5% of body weight, twice a day.
Feed only what koi can eat within 5 minutes.
Summer: feed 1 to 3 times daily. Spring and fall: feed a wheat germ-based food once every 2 days. Winter: koi often need no food.
Staple foods are daily pellets of 3–5 mm with at least 25% protein. Color foods have at least 36% protein plus spirulina, and some exceed 40%.
Young koi need more protein. Adults need a balanced diet with occasional treats such as lettuce, watermelon, shelled peas, worms or krill.
Overfeeding and a failed (dead) biological filter are common causes of rising ammonia.
Low oxygen in ponds is most common in the early morning. Other causes include cloudy weather, algal die-offs, excessive feeding and overstocking.
Koi ponds can become overstocked by accident when fish spawn and the offspring are kept.
Fish short of oxygen gather at the surface and gulp air, a behavior called piping.
Nitrite causes 'brown blood disease', and affected fish behave as if they are short of oxygen.
When ammonia is high, change at least 50% of the water and reduce or stop feeding.
For sudden nitrite spikes, salt may halt deaths, but water changes and filter maintenance are the main fixes.
Many ponds and aquaria keep 1–3 ppt residual salt, which makes nitrite toxicity less likely because chloride competes with nitrite at the gills.
The Vietnamese guide quarantines new or sick koi for 10–14 days in a separate tank with 20–30 cm of water and strong aeration.
For the quarantine tank, the same guide gives Elbagin or Tetra medicine at 1 g per 100 L and salt at 3–5 g per 1,000 L.
Un-ionized ammonia (NH3) of 0.05 mg/L harms gill tissue, and above 2 mg/L it is lethal for many fish. Toxicity rises with pH and temperature.
Chlorine can harm fish at 0.02 mg/L and kill at 0.04 mg/L. No chlorine or chloramine should be detectable while fish are present.
Removing chloramine releases ammonia, so test both free and total chlorine before and after treating the water.
Koi tolerate a wide temperature range, but drastic swings are still not acceptable. Sudden changes of even a few degrees can weaken immunity.
When handling or moving fish, keep temperature changes to about 1°C per hour.
Overfeeding makes fish obese and pollutes the water with leftover food.
Koi still eat in cool seasons even though they digest slowly, and this can cause problems over time.
Leaving food uneaten overnight lets it mold. Raw foods can spread pathogens.
Excess food degrades water quality and causes health problems.
In spring and summer, koi digest their food within 2 to 6 hours.
For outages: do not feed, because uneaten food adds nitrogen and most fish can go days or weeks without food.
During an outage in warm weather, clear objects off the water surface to improve gas exchange. Stirring the water, for example with a whisk, adds oxygen.
During an outage, change 10 to 30 percent of the water if ammonia goes above 1 ppm.
In heat, block direct sun. Fish usually tolerate the high 80s or low 90s °F for a day or more, but prolonged heat lowers oxygen.
If adding dechlorinated water during an outage, limit the temperature change to about 10 percent every hour or two.
